claim: BRCA2 is an essential protein in genome maintenance, homologous recombination (HR), and replication fork protection.
source: Breast cancer type two susceptibility protein (BRCA2) is an essential protein in genome maintenance, homologous recombination (HR), and replication fork protection.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established knowledge about BRCA2 function.

claim: BRCA2 knock-out is lethal in mammalian cells.
source: BRCA2 knock-out is lethal in mammalian cells, and a defective BRCA2 causes increased sensitivity to genotoxic agents, defective DNA repair, and reduced homologous recombination (HR) activity (Prakash et al., 2015; Sharan et al., 1997; Yu et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Defective BRCA2 causes increased sensitivity to genotoxic agents.
source: BRCA2 knock-out is lethal in mammalian cells, and a defective BRCA2 causes increased sensitivity to genotoxic agents, defective DNA repair, and reduced homologous recombination (HR) activity (Prakash et al., 2015; Sharan et al., 1997; Yu et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Defective BRCA2 causes defective DNA repair.
source: BRCA2 knock-out is lethal in mammalian cells, and a defective BRCA2 causes increased sensitivity to genotoxic agents, defective DNA repair, and reduced homologous recombination (HR) activity (Prakash et al., 2015; Sharan et al., 1997; Yu et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Defective BRCA2 causes reduced homologous recombination (HR) activity.
source: BRCA2 knock-out is lethal in mammalian cells, and a defective BRCA2 causes increased sensitivity to genotoxic agents, defective DNA repair, and reduced homologous recombination (HR) activity (Prakash et al., 2015; Sharan et al., 1997; Yu et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One role of BRCA2 common to DNA break repair, DNA crosslink repair, and replication fork protection is delivery of RAD51 to sites where it is needed.
source: One role of BRCA2 common to DNA break repair, DNA crosslink repair, and replication fork protection is delivery of RAD51 to sites where it is needed (Holloman, 2011; Sharan et al., 1997; Yuan et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RAD51 is an essential protein whose biochemical function is to form filaments on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) capable of performing strand exchange reactions with homologous partners or otherwise protecting the bound DNA.
source: RAD51 is also an essential protein whose biochemical function is to form filaments on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) capable of performing strand exchange reactions with homologous partners or otherwise protecting the bound DNA (Baumann and West, 1998; Heyer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The accumulation of RAD51 into foci depends on functional BRCA2.
source: The accumulation of RAD51 into foci depends on functional BRCA2 (Yuan et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The presence of Partner and Localizer of BRCA2 (PALB2) and its interaction with the N-terminus of BRCA2 are essential for the localization of BRCA2 and RAD51 to foci.
source: The presence of Partner and Localizer of BRCA2 (PALB2) and its interaction with the N-terminus of BRCA2 are essential for the localization of BRCA2 and RAD51 to foci (Oliver et al., 2009; Xia et al., 2007; Xia et al., 2006), whereas the loss of interaction affects HR and genome stability in general (Hartford et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The loss of interaction between PALB2 and BRCA2 affects HR and genome stability in general.
source: The presence of Partner and Localizer of BRCA2 (PALB2) and its interaction with the N-terminus of BRCA2 are essential for the localization of BRCA2 and RAD51 to foci (Oliver et al., 2009; Xia et al., 2007; Xia et al., 2006), whereas the loss of interaction affects HR and genome stability in general (Hartford et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In chicken DT40 cells, both N-terminal interaction with PALB2 and C-terminal DNA-binding domain (DBD) have a role in focal accumulation of BRCA2.
source: In chicken DT40 cells, both N-terminal interaction with PALB2 and C-terminal DNA-binding domain (DBD) have a role in focal accumulation of BRCA2; accumulation is fully eliminated if neither domain is present (Al Abo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Accumulation of BRCA2 is fully eliminated if neither N-terminal PALB2 interaction nor C-terminal DBD is present in chicken DT40 cells.
source: In chicken DT40 cells, both N-terminal interaction with PALB2 and C-terminal DNA-binding domain (DBD) have a role in focal accumulation of BRCA2; accumulation is fully eliminated if neither domain is present (Al Abo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The interaction of the BRCA2 DBD with the small DSS1 protein is required for proper localization of BRCA2 to the nucleus.
source: Additionally, the interaction of the BRCA2 DBD with the small DSS1 protein is required for proper localization of BRCA2 to the nucleus and for BRCA2 and RAD51 focus formation (Gudmundsdottir et al., 2004; Kojic et al., 2005; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The interaction of the BRCA2 DBD with the small DSS1 protein is required for BRCA2 and RAD51 focus formation.
source: Additionally, the interaction of the BRCA2 DBD with the small DSS1 protein is required for proper localization of BRCA2 to the nucleus and for BRCA2 and RAD51 focus formation (Gudmundsdottir et al., 2004; Kojic et al., 2005; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Single-particle tracking (SPT) in living mouse embryonic stem (mES) cells revealed that BRCA2 diffuses as multimeric complexes bound to all detectable nuclear RAD51.
source: Single-particle tracking (SPT) in living mouse embryonic stem (mES) cells revealed that BRCA2 diffuses as multimeric complexes bound to all detectable nuclear RAD51 (Reuter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Individual BRCA2 particles diffuse slowly and are transiently immobile.
source: Individual BRCA2 particles diffuse slowly and are transiently immobile, and this immobility increases in response to DNA-damage induction (Reuter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: BRCA2 immobility increases in response to DNA-damage induction.
source: Individual BRCA2 particles diffuse slowly and are transiently immobile, and this immobility increases in response to DNA-damage induction (Reuter et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: BRCA2 and RAD51 are separated at sites where they accumulate, as determined by super-resolution microscopy.
source: Although they diffuse together, BRCA2 and RAD51 are separated at sites where they accumulate, as determined by super-resolution microscopy (Sánchez et al., 2017; Whelan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Purified BRCA2 protein shows remarkable rearrangement by RAD51 and ssDNA.
source: Purified BRCA2 protein shows remarkable rearrangement by RAD51 and ssDNA (Le et al., 2020; Sánchez et al., 2017; Sidhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: BRCA2 has many predicted disordered regions.
source: BRCA2 has many predicted disordered regions, which complicate understanding the functional organization and possible dynamic rearrangement of the reported structured domains.
evidence: This is a statement about the structural properties of BRCA2 based on established knowledge.

claim: The largest crystallized segment of BRCA2 is the DBD (736 amino acids), which encompasses the helical domain, tower domain, and the three oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide binding (OB) folds.
source: Of these, the largest crystallized segment of BRCA2 is the DBD (736 amino acids), which encompasses the helical domain, tower domain, and the three oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide binding (OB) folds.
evidence: This claim is based on structural information from prior research.

claim: There are two distinct regions of BRCA2 that bind RAD51 with different consequences.
source: There are two distinct regions of BRCA2 that bind RAD51 with different consequences (Esashi et al., 2005; Galkin et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The eight centrally located BRC repeats bind multiple RAD51 molecules.
source: The eight centrally located BRC repeats bind multiple RAD51 molecules (Jensen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The BRC repeat-RAD51 interactions are important for localizing RAD51 into nuclear foci.
source: The BRC repeat-RAD51 interactions are important for localizing RAD51 into nuclear foci (Chen et al., 1999) and promoting RAD51 filament nucleation in vitro (Shahid et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The BRC repeat-RAD51 interactions promote RAD51 filament nucleation in vitro.
source: The BRC repeat-RAD51 interactions are important for localizing RAD51 into nuclear foci (Chen et al., 1999) and promoting RAD51 filament nucleation in vitro (Shahid et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is another RAD51-interaction domain at the C-terminus of BRCA2, which is inhibited by cell-cycle-regulated BRCA2 phosphorylation.
source: There is another RAD51-interaction domain at the C-terminus of BRCA2, which is inhibited by cell-cycle-regulated BRCA2 phosphorylation (Esashi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The C-terminal domain (CTD) of BRCA2, which is equivalent to exon 27, has a specific role in protecting replication forks.
source: This region, the C-terminal domain (CTD) of BRCA2, which is equivalent to exon 27, has a specific role in protecting replication forks (Feng and Jasin, 2017; Lomonosov et al., 2003; Schlacher et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The C-terminal RAD51-binding site is suggested to stimulate RAD51-mediated recombination and stabilize RAD51 filaments.
source: The C-terminal RAD51-binding site is also suggested to stimulate RAD51-mediated recombination and stabilize RAD51 filaments (Esashi et al., 2005) while the DBD in combination with DSS1 is suggested to exchange Replication protein A (RPA) for RAD51 on ssDNA (Yang et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DBD in combination with DSS1 is suggested to exchange Replication protein A (RPA) for RAD51 on ssDNA.
source: The C-terminal RAD51-binding site is also suggested to stimulate RAD51-mediated recombination and stabilize RAD51 filaments (Esashi et al., 2005) while the DBD in combination with DSS1 is suggested to exchange Replication protein A (RPA) for RAD51 on ssDNA (Yang et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DBD is not essential for cells to survive.
source: However, the DBD is not essential for cells to survive (Edwards et al., 2008), and although it is the most conserved part of BRCA2 (Yang et al., 2002), its exact cellular function remains elusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The DBD is the most conserved part of BRCA2.
source: However, the DBD is not essential for cells to survive (Edwards et al., 2008), and although it is the most conserved part of BRCA2 (Yang et al., 2002), its exact cellular function remains elusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The separate domains (DBD and CTD) do not play a significant role in BRCA2's nuclear localization and diffusion dynamics or RAD51 accumulation.
source: We discovered that the separate domains do not play a significant role in BRCA2's nuclear localization and diffusion dynamics or RAD51 accumulation but strongly affect protein conformational response to binding partners.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The separate domains (DBD and CTD) strongly affect protein conformational response to binding partners.
source: We discovered that the separate domains do not play a significant role in BRCA2's nuclear localization and diffusion dynamics or RAD51 accumulation but strongly affect protein conformational response to binding partners.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The BRCA2 conformational changes correlate with cellular HR activity.
source: The BRCA2 conformational changes correlate with cellular HR activity.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of CTD caused sensitization to IR (at 5 Gy up to fivefold decrease in surviving fraction, p<0.001), comparable to the effect of deleting the non-essential auxiliary HR protein RAD54.
source: Loss of CTD caused sensitization to IR (at 5 Gy up to fivefold decrease in surviving fraction, p<0.001), comparable to the effect of deleting the non-essential auxiliary HR protein RAD54 (Essers et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from clonogenic survival assays and includes a citation for comparison.

claim: Deletion of DBD further increased sensitization to IR (18-fold decrease in surviving fraction [p<0.001] or 3.6-fold more than in ∆CTD).
source: In contrast, deletion of DBD further increased sensitization to IR (18-fold decrease in surviving fraction [p<0.001] or 3.6-fold more than in ∆CTD), which was not further exacerbated if CTD was also missing (p<0.001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from clonogenic survival assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Deletion of DBD sensitization to IR was not further exacerbated if CTD was also missing.
source: In contrast, deletion of DBD further increased sensitization to IR (18-fold decrease in surviving fraction [p<0.001] or 3.6-fold more than in ∆CTD), which was not further exacerbated if CTD was also missing (p<0.001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from clonogenic survival assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Loss of CTD did not lead to a significant sensitization to cisplatin (p = 0.80).
source: Different from the results with IR and olaparib, loss of CTD did not lead to a significant sensitization to cisplatin (p = 0.80) nor MMC (p = 0.11) (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from clonogenic survival assays shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Loss of CTD did not lead to a significant sensitization to MMC (p = 0.11).
source: Different from the results with IR and olaparib, loss of CTD did not lead to a significant sensitization to cisplatin (p = 0.80) nor MMC (p = 0.11) (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from clonogenic survival assays shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The BRCA2 DBD is important for efficient HR-mediated DNA repair while the CTD is less critical for this cellular activity.
source: Together, these results indicate that the BRCA2 DBD is important for efficient HR-mediated DNA repair while the CTD is less critical for this cellular activity.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from clonogenic survival assays.

claim: The absolute gene-targeting frequency of about 5% was reduced twofold in BRCA2 ∆DBD (p = 0.0186) and ∆DBD∆CTD (p = 0.0021) cells.
source: The absolute gene-targeting frequency of about 5% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—source data 1) was reduced twofold in BRCA2 ∆DBD (p = 0.0186) and ∆DBD∆CTD (p = 0.0021) cells, while CTD deletion caused an intermediate effect (p = 0.0291).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the gene-targeting assay shown in Figure 1G and supplementary figures.

claim: CTD deletion caused an intermediate effect on gene-targeting frequency (p = 0.0291).
source: The absolute gene-targeting frequency of about 5% (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—source data 1) was reduced twofold in BRCA2 ∆DBD (p = 0.0186) and ∆DBD∆CTD (p = 0.0021) cells, while CTD deletion caused an intermediate effect (p = 0.0291).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the gene-targeting assay shown in Figure 1G and supplementary figures.

claim: DNA-damage sensitivity correlates with the gene-targeting assay, indicating that BRCA2 DBD is specifically important for HR activity at two-ended DNA breaks.
source: Thus, DNA-damage sensitivity described above correlates with this gene-targeting assay, indicating that BRCA2 DBD is specifically important for HR activity at two-ended DNA breaks.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the correlation between experimental data from clonogenic survival and gene-targeting assays.

claim: Formation of both spontaneous and IR-induced nuclear BRCA2 and RAD51 foci was observed in all three BRCA2 deletion variants.
source: However, we observed formation of both spontaneous and IR-induced nuclear BRCA2 and RAD51 foci in all three BRCA2 deletion variants, where BRCA2 and RAD51 foci appeared to overlap to a large extent (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2A.

claim: BRCA2 and RAD51 foci appeared to overlap to a large extent in all three BRCA2 deletion variants.
source: However, we observed formation of both spontaneous and IR-induced nuclear BRCA2 and RAD51 foci in all three BRCA2 deletion variants, where BRCA2 and RAD51 foci appeared to overlap to a large extent (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the absence of induced DNA damage (background), there was a reduction in BRCA2 foci number compared to full-length BRCA2 (20% reduction, p<0.001) only in the CTD deletion.
source: Only the CTD deletion affected BRCA2 foci, and in the absence of induced DNA damage (background), there was a reduction in their number compared to full-length BRCA2 (20% reduction, p<0.001) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of BRCA2 foci shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Upon irradiation, the number of BRCA2 foci increased in all deletion variants (p<0.001 for all BRCA2 variants).
source: Upon irradiation, the number of BRCA2 foci increased in all deletion variants, (p<0.001 for all BRCA2 variants).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of BRCA2 foci.

claim: The total number of BRCA2 foci appeared lower than full-length after radiation in all deletion variants.
source: However, total number of BRCA2 foci appeared lower than full-length after radiation in all deletion variants.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of BRCA2 foci.

claim: The effect of DBD and CTD deletion on the intensity of background BRCA2 foci was much more pronounced (1.5-fold reduction, p<0.001).
source: The effect of DBD and CTD deletion on the intensity of background BRCA2 foci was much more pronounced (1.5-fold reduction, p<0.001) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of BRCA2 foci intensity shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In all cell lines, IR-induced increase in the number of foci was accompanied by a decrease in focus intensity.
source: Interestingly, in all cell lines, IR-induced increase in the number of foci was accompanied by a decrease in focus intensity, suggesting that BRCA2 re-localizes from the background to the IR-induced foci, but this effect was suppressed in the deletion variants (only 13% reduction in ∆DBD compared to 26% in cells expressing full-length BRCA2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of BRCA2 foci.

claim: BRCA2 re-localizes from the background to the IR-induced foci.
source: Interestingly, in all cell lines, IR-induced increase in the number of foci was accompanied by a decrease in focus intensity, suggesting that BRCA2 re-localizes from the background to the IR-induced foci, but this effect was suppressed in the deletion variants (only 13% reduction in ∆DBD compared to 26% in cells expressing full-length BRCA2).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the number of foci increases while intensity decreases.

claim: The effect of BRCA2 re-localization from background to IR-induced foci was suppressed in the deletion variants (only 13% reduction in ∆DBD compared to 26% in cells expressing full-length BRCA2).
source: Interestingly, in all cell lines, IR-induced increase in the number of foci was accompanied by a decrease in focus intensity, suggesting that BRCA2 re-localizes from the background to the IR-induced foci, but this effect was suppressed in the deletion variants (only 13% reduction in ∆DBD compared to 26% in cells expressing full-length BRCA2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of BRCA2 foci.

claim: The number of RAD51 foci increased in both deletion variants and the control cells (p<0.001 for all BRCA2 variants).
source: As with BRCA2 foci, the number of RAD51 foci increased in both deletion variants and the control cells (p<0.001 for all BRCA2 variants).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of RAD51 foci.

claim: The number of RAD51 foci peaked 2 hr after IR in wild-type ES cells, then gradually decreased over time reaching near-background levels at 24 hr.
source: Consistent with our previous observations in wild-type ES cells, the number of RAD51 foci peaked 2 hr after IR, then gradually decreased over time reaching near-background levels at 24 hr (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of RAD51 foci shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: For the ∆DBD cells, the number of RAD51 foci increased but did not decrease over time, remaining high at 24 hr.
source: For the ∆DBD cells, the number of foci increased but did not decrease over time, remaining high at 24 hr.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of RAD51 foci.

claim: The return to background number of RAD51 foci was suppressed to a lesser extent in ∆CTD and the double mutant.
source: The return to background number of foci was suppressed to a lesser extent in ∆CTD and the double mutant.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of RAD51 foci.

claim: In the control cells, changes in RAD51 foci intensity paralleled changes in their number: peaking at 2 hr, decreasing gradually thereafter.
source: In the control cells, changes in RAD51 foci intensity paralleled changes in their number: peaking at 2 hr, decreasing gradually thereafter (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of RAD51 foci intensity shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In all the three deletion variants, RAD51 focus intensity increase was reduced (1.2-fold increase compared to 2-fold in control) or delayed (peak at 8 hr compared to 2 hr in control).
source: In all the three deletion variants, focus intensity increase was reduced (1.2-fold increase compared to 2-fold in control) or delayed (peak at 8 hr compared to 2 hr in control) (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from quantification of RAD51 foci intensity shown in Figure 2F,G.

claim: The deletion mutants of BRCA2 do accumulate RAD51 proteins to IR-induced lesions; however, less RAD51 accumulates and its turnover is suppressed.
source: Taken together, these results show that the deletion mutants of BRCA2 do accumulate RAD51 proteins to IR-induced lesions; however, less RAD51 accumulates and its turnover is supressed.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from RAD51 foci quantification.

claim: BRCA2 deletion variants all had a similar apparent diffusion coefficient; mobile molecules diffuse with a rate similar to the full-length protein.
source: The BRCA2 deletion variants all had a similar apparent diffusion coefficient; mobile molecules diffuse with a rate similar to the full-length protein (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from single-particle tracking shown in Figure 3D and supplementary figures.

claim: The increase in immobile tracklets after IR for the variants BRCA2 ΔDBD and ΔCTD was similar to full-length, indicating that these domains separately are not essential for this change in mobility.
source: The increase in immobile tracklets after IR for the variants BRCA2 ΔDBD and ΔCTD was similar to full-length, indicating that these domains separately are not essential for this change in mobility (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from single-particle tracking shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The immobile fraction for BRCA2 ΔDBDΔCTD, missing both regions, did not increase after IR as much as the others (3% increase compared to 7–10%).
source: However, the immobile fraction for BRCA2 ΔDBDΔCTD, missing both regions, did not increase after IR as much as the others (3% increase compared to 7–10%; Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from single-particle tracking shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Either DBD or CTD is sufficient for BRCA2 mobility changes in response to IR but a protein missing both of these domains reduces this response.
source: Thus, either DBD or CTD is sufficient for BRCA2 mobility changes in response to IR but a protein missing both of these domains reduces this response.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from single-particle tracking.

claim: Diffusion changes in response to DNA damage were not sufficient to assure cell survival or proper HR activity.
source: As deletion of single domains, ΔDBD or ΔCTD, did cause increased sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents (Figure 1), we can conclude that diffusion changes in response to DNA damage were not sufficient to assure cell survival or proper HR activity.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from clonogenic survival and single-particle tracking.

claim: All three BRCA2 deletion variants exist as a distribution of irregular oligomeric molecules as previously observed for the full-length protein.
source: All three BRCA2 deletion variants exist as a distribution of irregular oligomeric molecules as previously observed for the full-length protein (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Sánchez et al., 2017; Sidhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 4A,B and supplementary figures, with citations to prior research.

claim: In the conditions used, the majority (70%) of full-length BRCA2 was present as assemblies larger than tetramers.
source: In the conditions used here, the majority (70%) of full-length BRCA2 was present as assemblies larger than tetramers (Figure 4B, left panel).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The C-terminal deletion variants showed reduced oligomerization for all the variants with 46% BRCA2 ΔDBD, 54% BRCA2 ΔCTD, and 44% BRCA2 ΔDBDΔCTD present as assemblies larger than tetramers.
source: The C-terminal deletion variants showed reduced oligomerization for all the variants with 46% BRCA2 ΔDBD, 54% BRCA2 ΔCTD, and 44% BRCA2 ΔDBDΔCTD present as assemblies larger than tetramers (Figure 4B, left panel and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 4B and supplementary figures.

claim: Decrease in large oligomers coincides with an increase in the monomer population from <10% in full-length to ~30% in BRCA2 ΔDBDΔCTD.
source: Decrease in large oligomers coincides with an increase in the monomer population from <10% in full-length to ~30% in BRCA2 ΔDBDΔCTD (Figure 4B, left panel), indicating that both DBD and CTD contribute to BRCA2 interactions with itself, at least in the absence of other binding partners.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both DBD and CTD contribute to BRCA2 interactions with itself, at least in the absence of other binding partners.
source: Decrease in large oligomers coincides with an increase in the monomer population from <10% in full-length to ~30% in BRCA2 ΔDBDΔCTD (Figure 4B, left panel), indicating that both DBD and CTD contribute to BRCA2 interactions with itself, at least in the absence of other binding partners.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from scanning force microscopy.

claim: Upon incubation with RAD51, full-length BRCA2 assemblies become largely monomeric (74%) and adopt a more regular compact conformation, with 33% having a rod-like shape (major to minor axis ratio >1.5).
source: Upon incubation with RAD51, full-length BRCA2 assemblies become largely monomeric (74%) and adopt a more regular compact conformation, with 33% having a rod-like shape (major to minor axis ratio >1.5) (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 4A,B and supplementary figures.

claim: Purified BRCA2 binds six RAD51 monomers in conditions similar to ours.
source: Purified BRCA2 binds six RAD51 monomers in conditions similar to ours (Jensen et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: All deletion variants also become largely monomeric upon interaction with RAD51, but to a lesser extent than the full-length BRCA2 (40–55% for variants vs 74% for full-length).
source: All deletion variants also become largely monomeric upon interaction with RAD51, but to a lesser extent than the full-length BRCA2 (40–55% for variants vs 74% for full-length).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy.

claim: All the variants included about one-third of the complexes as dimers: BRCA2 ΔDBD (28%), BRCA2 ΔCTD (32%), and BRCA2 ΔDBDΔCTD (33%), which was more than the full-length BRCA2 (18%).
source: However, all the variants included about one-third of the complexes as dimers: BRCA2 ΔDBD (28%), BRCA2 ΔCTD (32%), and BRCA2 ΔDBDΔCTD (33%), which was more than the full-length BRCA2 (18%) (Figure 4B,C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Only BRCA2 ΔCTD-RAD51 formed rod-shaped assemblies similar to full-length BRCA2.
source: Only BRCA2 ΔCTD-RAD51 formed rod-shaped assemblies similar to full-length BRCA2 (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Removing either DBD, CTD, or both reduced BRCA2 oligomerization and, to a lesser extent, reduced RAD51-induced changes in oligomerization and architecture.
source: Removing either DBD, CTD, or both reduced BRCA2 oligomerization and, to a lesser extent, reduced RAD51-induced changes in oligomerization and architecture (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Full-length BRCA2 is present in oligomeric complexes with extensions, in a bimodal distribution of solidity with peaks at 0.75 and 0.95.
source: Full-length BRCA2 is present in oligomeric complexes with extensions, in a bimodal distribution of solidity—a measure of the compactness of the protein complexes—with peaks at 0.75 and 0.95 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Incubation with ssDNA shifts the solidity distribution of full-length BRCA2 to a single peak at 0.7.
source: Incubation with ssDNA shifts the solidity distribution to a single peak at 0.7 (Figure 5; FL BRCA2 + ssDNA).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 5.

claim: The BRCA2 C-terminal deletion variants had fewer extended molecules to begin with, as solidity shows a peak distribution around 0.9 for all the three variants; ΔDBD, ΔCTD, and ΔDBDΔCTD.
source: The BRCA2 C-terminal deletion variants had fewer extended molecules to begin with, as solidity shows a peak distribution around 0.9 for all the three variants; ΔDBD, ΔCTD, and ΔDBDΔCTD (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 5.

claim: In striking contrast to the full-length BRCA2, interaction with ssDNA did not change the distribution of oligomers and shape (solidity) for any of the deletion variants.
source: In striking contrast to the full-length BRCA2, interaction with ssDNA did not change the distribution of oligomers and shape (solidity) for any of the deletion variants (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Both DBD and CTD have to be present for BRCA2 to undergo the conformational change associated with ssDNA interactions.
source: Both DBD and CTD have to be present for BRCA2 to undergo the conformational change associated with ssDNA interactions.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from scanning force microscopy.

claim: The effect of the BRCA2 DBD and CTD domain deletions on cellular response to DNA damage and their effect on the architecture of BRCA2 and its complexes with RAD51 and ssDNA did correlate.
source: The effect of the BRCA2 DBD and CTD domain deletions on cellular response to DNA damage (Figures 1–3) and their effect on the architecture of BRCA2 and its complexes with RAD51 and ssDNA did correlate.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from cellular assays and scanning force microscopy.

claim: The architectural changes defined in this study may report on important BRCA2 cellular functions.
source: The architectural changes we defined here may report on important BRCA2 cellular functions.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: A substantial reduction in DNA-damage resistance, especially in DBD-deficient cells, was accompanied by only subtle changes in dynamics and localization of BRCA2.
source: We found that a substantial reduction in DNA-damage resistance, especially in DBD-deficient cells, was accompanied by only subtle changes in dynamics and localization of BRCA2.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data from cellular assays and single-particle tracking.

claim: The ability of purified recombinant BRCA2 to undergo structural rearrangements was strongly affected by DBD or CTD deletions.
source: In contrast, the ability of purified recombinant BRCA2 to undergo structural rearrangements was strongly affected by DBD or CTD deletions (Table 1, Table 2).
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data from scanning force microscopy summarized in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Despite their adjacent location in the C-terminal part of BRCA2, DBD and CTD are functionally distinct.
source: Despite their adjacent location in the C-terminal part of BRCA2 (and frequent simultaneous loss due to human cancer-predisposing mutations), DBD and CTD are functionally distinct.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing different effects of DBD and CTD deletions.

claim: In mouse BRCA2, an additional nuclear localization signal is present at the N-terminus.
source: In mouse BRCA2, an additional nuclear localization signal is present at the N-terminus, but in the human protein, there is no such redundancy, which exaggerates the consequence of even short C-terminal truncations, because these produce human BRCA2 that cannot localize to the nucleus (Sarkisian et al., 2001; Spain et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the human protein, there is no redundancy of nuclear localization signals, which exaggerates the consequence of even short C-terminal truncations, because these produce human BRCA2 that cannot localize to the nucleus.
source: In mouse BRCA2, an additional nuclear localization signal is present at the N-terminus, but in the human protein, there is no such redundancy, which exaggerates the consequence of even short C-terminal truncations, because these produce human BRCA2 that cannot localize to the nucleus (Sarkisian et al., 2001; Spain et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DBD is the evolutionarily defining part of BRCA2, conserved from fungi to humans.
source: The DBD is the evolutionarily defining part of BRCA2, conserved from fungi to humans, but its function is less defined than that of other 'younger' BRCA2 regions.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about BRCA2 evolution.

claim: Despite its deep phylogenetic roots, the DBD is not what makes BRCA2 essential for general viability of animal cells.
source: Our findings reinforce the notion that despite its deep phylogenetic roots, the DBD is not what makes BRCA2 essential for general viability of animal cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing that cells can survive without DBD.

claim: Absence of the DBD leads to significant sensitization to DNA interstrand crosslinks, PARP inhibitor, and radiation, not further exacerbated by additional CTD deletion.
source: Absence of the DBD leads to significant sensitization to DNA interstrand crosslinks, PARP inhibitor, and radiation, not further exacerbated by additional CTD deletion (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from clonogenic survival assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: DSS1 interaction is required for BRCA2 stability and intracellular localization.
source: On the one hand, it is as conserved as the DBD itself, and it was shown to be required for BRCA2 stability and intracellular localization (Li et al., 2006); mutations in DSS1 binding phenocopy BRCA2 deficiency, as does DSS1 depletion (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mutations in DSS1 binding phenocopy BRCA2 deficiency, as does DSS1 depletion.
source: On the one hand, it is as conserved as the DBD itself, and it was shown to be required for BRCA2 stability and intracellular localization (Li et al., 2006); mutations in DSS1 binding phenocopy BRCA2 deficiency, as does DSS1 depletion (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In fungi, DSS1 is only required for DNA repair when DBD is present.
source: But, on the other hand, in fungi, DSS1 is only required for DNA repair when DBD is present (Kojic et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In human cells, HR could be partially restored in BRCA2-deficient cells by complementation with variants lacking the DBD.
source: Similarly, in human cells, HR could be partially restored in BRCA2-deficient cells by complementation with variants lacking the DBD (Edwards et al., 2008; Siaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cells expressing BRCA2 ΔDBD retained ~50% of HR activity.
source: Our results also show that cells expressing BRCA2 ΔDBD retained ~50% of HR activity (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from the gene-targeting assay shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In cells that lack BRCA2 DBD (ΔDBD and ΔDBDΔCTD), there is an increased number of RAD51 foci in the untreated condition (p<0.001).
source: In cells that lack BRCA2 DBD (ΔDBD and ΔDBDΔCTD), we do observe an increased number of RAD51 foci in the untreated condition (p<0.001), which could indicate increased replication-associated DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from RAD51 foci quantification.

claim: The increased number of RAD51 foci in cells lacking BRCA2 DBD could indicate increased replication-associated DNA damage.
source: In cells that lack BRCA2 DBD (ΔDBD and ΔDBDΔCTD), we do observe an increased number of RAD51 foci in the untreated condition (p<0.001), which could indicate increased replication-associated DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: The increased number of RAD51 foci in cells lacking BRCA2 DBD did not affect the growth rate of the cells.
source: This, however, did not affect the growth rate of the cells.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observation.

claim: The DBD does not have a significant role in the context of constrained diffusion of BRCA2.
source: We also found that DBD contributes little to the characteristic constrained diffusion we described previously. Binding of the DBD to DNA could explain slow diffusion and frequent immobilization of BRCA2—with a higher frequency after damage induction. But the effect of loss of DBD on diffusive activity was small and comparable to loss of CTD. Therefore, we conclude that the DBD does not have a significant role in this context.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from single-particle tracking.

claim: In the BRCA2-containing complex, DNA-binding activity could be redundantly supplied by its interactors.
source: In the BRCA2-containing complex, DNA-binding activity could be redundantly supplied by its interactors. For example, several BRCA2-bound RAD51 molecules provide alternative DNA interaction interfaces (Jensen et al., 2010; Reuter et al., 2014; Sánchez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: Several BRCA2-bound RAD51 molecules provide alternative DNA interaction interfaces.
source: For example, several BRCA2-bound RAD51 molecules provide alternative DNA interaction interfaces (Jensen et al., 2010; Reuter et al., 2014; Sánchez et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In contrast to the DBD, the CTD is a recent vertebrate addition to BRCA2.
source: In contrast to the DBD, the CTD is a recent vertebrate addition to BRCA2.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about BRCA2 evolution.

claim: CTD deletion resulted in no phenotype (interstrand crosslink survival), intermediate phenotype (radiation and PARPi survival, HR assay, RAD51 focus number), or the same effect as DBD deletion (RAD51 focus intensity).
source: In our assays, its deletion resulted in no phenotype (interstrand crosslink survival), intermediate phenotype (radiation and PARPi survival, HR assay, RAD51 focus number), or the same effect as DBD deletion (RAD51 focus intensity).
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data from various cellular assays.

claim: Except for BRCA2 oligomerization, deleting both domains did not result in an additive effect.
source: Except for BRCA2 oligomerization (Figure 4B), deleting both domains did not result in an additive effect.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental data from various cellular assays and scanning force microscopy.

claim: The strongest argument against CTD deletion encroaching on or disturbing the structure of the DBD is the clear separation of functions between the domains in the interstrand crosslink survival assays where CTD deletion has no effect.
source: It is possible that CTD deletion we created encroaches on or disturbs the structure of the DBD, and (some of) the functional consequences we attribute to the CTD deletion result from collateral damage to the DBD. The strongest argument against this is the clear separation of functions between the domains in the interstrand crosslink survival assays (Figure 1E,F) where CTD deletion has no effect.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from clonogenic survival assays.

claim: The described fork protection and RAD51 filament stabilization functions of the CTD are not essential for DNA crosslink repair.
source: This finding also suggests that the described fork protection and RAD51 filament stabilization functions of the CTD are not essential for DNA crosslink repair.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from clonogenic survival assays.

claim: CTD deletion blocked structural rearrangements of BRCA2 upon interaction with ssDNA as efficiently as the DBD deletion.
source: Another unexpected observation was that CTD deletion blocked structural rearrangements of BRCA2 upon interaction with ssDNA as efficiently as the DBD deletion.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy.

claim: N-C terminal interactions that contribute to oligomerization of BRCA2 also affect BRCA2 structure and thereby influence the BRCA2-ssDNA interaction.
source: One possibility is that N-C terminal interactions that contribute to oligomerization of BRCA2 (Le et al., 2020) also affect BRCA2 structure and thereby influence the BRCA2-ssDNA interaction.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental data and a citation to prior research.

claim: BRCA2 ΔCTD cells are sensitive to IR and PARP inhibitors but are not sensitive to DNA-crosslinking agents (MMC and cisplatin).
source: Finally, it is interesting to note that BRCA2 ΔCTD cells in our hands are sensitive to IR and PARP inhibitors but are not sensitive to DNA-crosslinking agents (MMC and cisplatin); this could indicate that these structural rearrangements are more relevant in the context of BRCA2's function in repair in two-ended double-strand breaks than during repair of DNA crosslinks, possibly due to other interacting proteins during crosslink repair.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from clonogenic survival assays.

claim: The structural rearrangements of BRCA2 are more relevant in the context of BRCA2's function in repair in two-ended double-strand breaks than during repair of DNA crosslinks, possibly due to other interacting proteins during crosslink repair.
source: Finally, it is interesting to note that BRCA2 ΔCTD cells in our hands are sensitive to IR and PARP inhibitors but are not sensitive to DNA-crosslinking agents (MMC and cisplatin); this could indicate that these structural rearrangements are more relevant in the context of BRCA2's function in repair in two-ended double-strand breaks than during repair of DNA crosslinks, possibly due to other interacting proteins during crosslink repair.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: RAD51 focus formation was observed in cell lines that were deficient in HR at two-ended double-strand breaks.
source: We observed RAD51 focus formation in cell lines that were, however, deficient in HR at two-ended double-strand breaks.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from RAD51 foci quantification and gene-targeting assays.

claim: The reduced intensity of RAD51 foci in cells lacking DBD and CTD indicates that the repair process is delayed or reduced at some point beyond delivery of RAD51 by BRCA2 to the sites of damage.
source: The reduced intensity of RAD51 foci in cells lacking DBD and CTD indicates that the repair process is delayed or reduced at some point beyond delivery of RAD51 by BRCA2 to the sites of damage.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from RAD51 foci quantification.

claim: RAD51 foci quantification could occasionally return false-positive results for HR function at two-ended breaks.
source: This suggests that RAD51 foci quantification, although useful to identify more HR-deficient samples than BRCA1/2 mutations, could occasionally return false-positive results for HR function at two-ended breaks.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: In the context of employing the RAD51 focus-formation assay in pre-clinical and clinical settings with the aim to find BRCAness phenotypes, identification of additional HR markers will be of value.
source: However, in the context of employing the RAD51 focus-formation assay in pre-clinical and clinical settings with the aim to find BRCAness phenotypes, identification of additional HR markers will be of value.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: The DBD and CTD of BRCA2 markedly affected protein architecture and conformational changes in response to binding partners.
source: The DBD and CTD of BRCA2 did markedly affect protein architecture and conformational changes in response to binding partners.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy.

claim: DBD and CTD contributed to oligomerization, when removed, and in DBD and CTD deletion variants, the BRCA2 population was less oligomeric.
source: These domains contributed to oligomerization, when we removed them, and in DBD and CTD deletion variants, the BRCA2 population was less oligomeric.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy.

claim: Interaction of N- and C-terminal fragments of BRCA2 contributes to oligomerization of BRCA2.
source: This is in agreement with a recent study where interaction of N- and C-terminal fragments of BRCA2 is indicated to contribute to oligomerization of BRCA2 (Le et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The oligomeric forms induced by RAD51 binding remain unchanged, which is likely mediated by the interaction with the intact BRC repeats.
source: However, in our study, the oligomeric forms induced by RAD51 binding remain unchanged, which is likely mediated by the interaction with the intact BRC repeats.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from scanning force microscopy.

claim: The characteristic conformational change of irregular compact particles to the extended architecture of full-length BRCA2 in response to ssDNA was severely impaired in all the investigated deletion variants.
source: The characteristic conformational change of irregular compact particles to the extended architecture of full-length BRCA2 in response to ssDNA was severely impaired in all the investigated deletion variants.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data from scanning force microscopy.

claim: The inability of the deletion variants to rearrange in vitro in the presence of ssDNA coupled with impaired HR in vivo suggests that DBD and CTD interactions of BRCA2 are important for optimal BRCA2 activity at the sites of damage.
source: Together, the inability of the deletion variants to rearrange in vitro in the presence of ssDNA coupled with impaired HR in vivo suggests that DBD and CTD interactions of BRCA2 are important for optimal BRCA2 activity at the sites of damage.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from scanning force microscopy and cellular assays.

claim: DSS1 affects the conformation of BRCA2.
source: A similar regulatory function is reported for other proteins that interact with BRCA2 such as DSS1, which also affects the conformation of BRCA2 (Le et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Regulation of oligomerization of BRCA2 is relevant in cells.
source: A recent study confirmed that regulation of oligomerization of BRCA2 is also relevant in cells, and variants of unknown significance with mutations in the DBD that reduce the binding of DSS1 show reduced nuclear localization and appear to increase/reduce oligomerization of BRCA2 (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Variants of unknown significance with mutations in the DBD that reduce the binding of DSS1 show reduced nuclear localization and appear to increase/reduce oligomerization of BRCA2.
source: A recent study confirmed that regulation of oligomerization of BRCA2 is also relevant in cells, and variants of unknown significance with mutations in the DBD that reduce the binding of DSS1 show reduced nuclear localization and appear to increase/reduce oligomerization of BRCA2 (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Regulation of RAD51 by BRCA2 is affected by conformational rearrangement of BRCA2 and is mediated at different levels by self-interaction of BRCA2 and its interaction partners.
source: Altogether, these and our study suggests that regulation of RAD51 by BRCA2 is affected by conformational rearrangement of BRCA2 and is mediated at different levels by self-interaction of BRCA2 and its interaction partners.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: Although none of the molecular endpoints analyzed (diffusion, foci, architecture) correlated perfectly with the functional outcomes (survival and recombination assay), the magnitude of the effect on architectural plasticity was the closest reflection.
source: Comparing all the molecular endpoints we analyzed (diffusion, foci, architecture), we conclude that although none correlated perfectly with the functional outcomes (survival and recombination assay), the magnitude of the effect on architectural plasticity was the closest reflection.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data from various assays.

claim: BRCA2 function may depend not so much on the existence of one structural form or another but on the lifetime of specific conformations affected by its interactors and local chromatin organization.
source: BRCA2 function may depend not so much on the existence of one structural form or another but on the lifetime of specific conformations affected by its interactors and local chromatin organization, parameters that will need to be quantified.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental data.
